title: Chemistry Practical III
source_note: 300L integrated practical chemistry curriculum covering volumetric/gravimetric analysis, qualitative inorganic analysis, organic practical techniques (recrystallisation, melting point, extraction, simple chromatography), and physical chemistry practicals (kinetics, conductometry, pH titration, viscometry), with emphasis on technique, safety, calibration, and data/error handling.

questions.question: Before use, a burette should be rinsed with a small quantity of:
options: Distilled water only, leaving it wet
The titrant solution itself, to avoid dilution of the titrant by residual water
Any convenient laboratory solvent
Concentrated acid regardless of the titrant used
questions.correct_answer: The titrant solution itself, to avoid dilution of the titrant by residual water
questions.explanation: Rinsing the burette with the titrant ensures any residual water is displaced, preventing dilution of the titrant and inaccurate volume readings.

questions.question: When reading the meniscus of an aqueous solution in a burette, the correct practice is to read at:
options: The top of the meniscus
Eye level, at the bottom of the meniscus curve
Any convenient angle above the liquid surface
The point where the meniscus touches the glass wall
questions.correct_answer: Eye level, at the bottom of the meniscus curve
questions.explanation: Reading at eye level at the bottom of the concave meniscus avoids parallax error and gives an accurate volume reading for aqueous solutions.

questions.question: In an acid-base titration, the indicator is chosen so that its colour change (end point) occurs:
options: Exactly at the stoichiometric equivalence point or as close to it as possible within the steep part of the pH curve
At pH 7 regardless of the acid/base strengths involved
Before any titrant has been added
Only after excess titrant has been added well past equivalence
questions.correct_answer: Exactly at the stoichiometric equivalence point or as close to it as possible within the steep part of the pH curve
questions.explanation: A suitable indicator's transition range should fall within the sharp pH jump around the equivalence point so the observed end point closely matches the true equivalence point.

questions.question: In a gravimetric determination, after precipitation the precipitate is typically washed with a dilute electrolyte solution rather than pure water mainly to:
options: Increase the solubility of the precipitate
Prevent peptisation (redispersion) of the colloidal precipitate
Add extra mass to the precipitate
Change the precipitate's chemical identity
questions.correct_answer: Prevent peptisation (redispersion) of the colloidal precipitate
questions.explanation: Washing with pure water can strip counter-ions from a colloidal precipitate, causing peptisation (particles redisperse and pass through the filter); a dilute electrolyte wash solution prevents this while still removing impurities.

questions.question: A gravimetric precipitate is dried or ignited to constant weight primarily to ensure that:
options: All moisture and volatile impurities are removed and the precipitate has a well-defined, reproducible composition
The precipitate changes colour for identification
The crucible mass increases indefinitely
The precipitate becomes soluble again
questions.correct_answer: All moisture and volatile impurities are removed and the precipitate has a well-defined, reproducible composition
questions.explanation: Repeated heating and weighing until the mass no longer changes confirms complete removal of water/volatiles and conversion to a stable, stoichiometrically defined weighing form.

questions.question: In qualitative inorganic analysis, dilute hydrochloric acid is added first to a solution to test for cations of which group because it selectively precipitates:
options: Group I cations (Ag+, Pb2+, Hg2^2+) as insoluble chlorides
All cations present in solution
Only sulfate ions
Only carbonate ions
questions.correct_answer: Group I cations (Ag+, Pb2+, Hg2^2+) as insoluble chlorides
questions.explanation: Dilute HCl selectively precipitates Ag+, Pb2+, and Hg2^2+ as insoluble chlorides (Group I in the classical qualitative analysis scheme), separating them from other cations before further group tests.

questions.question: In qualitative analysis, passing hydrogen sulfide gas into an acidified solution is used to precipitate cations of Group II (e.g. Cu2+, Pb2+, Hg2+, Cd2+) as insoluble:
options: Sulfates
Sulfides
Chlorides
Carbonates
questions.correct_answer: Sulfides
questions.explanation: In acidic solution, H2S precipitates Group II cations as their characteristically insoluble metal sulfides, distinguishing this group from later groups precipitated under different conditions.

questions.question: A flame test showing a brick-red colouration is most indicative of the presence of which cation?
options: Sodium
Potassium
Calcium
Barium
questions.correct_answer: Calcium
questions.explanation: Calcium salts impart a characteristic brick-red flame colour, distinguishing calcium from sodium (yellow), potassium (lilac), and barium (apple-green) in flame tests.

questions.question: The brown ring test is used to confirm the presence of which anion in a sample?
options: Chloride
Nitrate
Sulfate
Carbonate
questions.correct_answer: Nitrate
questions.explanation: Adding freshly prepared iron(II) sulfate solution followed by carefully layered concentrated sulfuric acid produces a brown ring of [Fe(NO)(H2O)5]2+ at the interface, confirming nitrate.

questions.question: Effervescence and formation of a gas that turns limewater milky, when a carbonate salt is treated with dilute acid, confirms the release of:
options: Hydrogen gas
Carbon dioxide gas
Oxygen gas
Chlorine gas
questions.correct_answer: Carbon dioxide gas
questions.explanation: Carbonates react with dilute acid to release CO2, which turns limewater (calcium hydroxide solution) milky due to formation of insoluble calcium carbonate.

questions.question: In recrystallisation as a purification technique for an organic solid, the ideal solvent should dissolve the compound readily when hot but:
options: Also dissolve it readily when cold
Dissolve it poorly when cold, so the compound crystallises out on cooling
Never dissolve the impurities at all
React chemically with the compound
questions.correct_answer: Dissolve it poorly when cold, so the compound crystallises out on cooling
questions.explanation: An ideal recrystallisation solvent shows a large difference in solubility between hot and cold conditions, allowing the compound to crystallise out in pure form upon cooling while impurities remain dissolved.

questions.question: Hot filtration is used during recrystallisation mainly to:
options: Remove insoluble impurities before the desired compound crystallises out on cooling
Cool the solution rapidly
Increase the yield of impurities
Dissolve the filter paper
questions.correct_answer: Remove insoluble impurities before the desired compound crystallises out on cooling
questions.explanation: Filtering the hot, saturated solution removes insoluble impurities while the desired compound remains dissolved, preventing loss of product and ensuring a purer crystalline product upon cooling.

questions.question: A sharp melting point with a narrow range (e.g. 1-2 degC) for a recrystallised organic solid generally indicates:
options: The compound is highly impure
The compound is relatively pure
The compound has decomposed
The melting point apparatus is faulty
questions.correct_answer: The compound is relatively pure
questions.explanation: Impurities generally lower and broaden the melting point range; a sharp, narrow melting range close to the literature value is evidence of high purity.

questions.question: In a mixed melting point determination, if an unknown compound is suspected to be identical to a known sample, mixing the two and observing:
options: A raised, sharper melting point confirms they are identical
No depression of the melting point (it remains sharp, similar to the individual samples) supports that they are the same compound
Any melting point change confirms they are different regardless of direction
The colour of the mixture alone confirms identity
questions.correct_answer: No depression of the melting point (it remains sharp, similar to the individual samples) supports that they are the same compound
questions.explanation: If two samples are the same substance, mixing them does not act as an impurity to each other, so the melting point remains sharp and undepressed; different compounds normally lower and broaden the mixed melting point.

questions.question: In a solvent extraction using a separating funnel, after shaking and allowing the layers to settle, the denser (lower) layer is removed by:
options: Pouring from the top of the funnel
Opening the stopcock at the bottom and draining it off, then closing the stopcock before the upper layer reaches it
Evaporating the entire mixture
Filtering through paper without separating the layers
questions.correct_answer: Opening the stopcock at the bottom and draining it off, then closing the stopcock before the upper layer reaches it
questions.explanation: The denser layer settles at the bottom and is drained through the stopcock; the tap is closed as soon as the interface reaches it to avoid mixing the two layers.

questions.question: In thin layer chromatography practical work, the sample spot must be applied above the level of the developing solvent in the chamber because:
options: Otherwise the spotted compound would dissolve directly into the solvent reservoir rather than being carried up the plate by capillary action
The spot needs to be as low as possible for best results
It has no effect on the chromatogram
The solvent evaporates faster at higher spots
questions.correct_answer: Otherwise the spotted compound would dissolve directly into the solvent reservoir rather than being carried up the plate by capillary action
questions.explanation: If the spot is submerged in the solvent, the sample washes off directly into the reservoir instead of being developed up the plate, ruining the separation.

questions.question: In a kinetics practical measuring the rate of reaction between sodium thiosulfate and hydrochloric acid (the 'disappearing cross' method), the time recorded is used to calculate a quantity proportional to rate, typically taken as:
options: The time itself
1/time
Time squared
The square root of time
questions.correct_answer: 1/time
questions.explanation: Since the reaction produces a fixed amount of sulfur needed to obscure the cross, a shorter time indicates a faster reaction, so 1/time is used as a relative measure of rate.

questions.question: In a practical determining the order of a reaction using the initial rates method, the reaction is repeated multiple times while:
options: Keeping all reactant concentrations exactly the same in each run
Systematically varying the concentration of one reactant at a time while keeping others constant
Only varying the temperature
Only varying the volume of the reaction vessel
questions.correct_answer: Systematically varying the concentration of one reactant at a time while keeping others constant
questions.explanation: Varying one reactant's concentration while holding others fixed isolates its effect on the initial rate, allowing the order with respect to that reactant to be determined.

questions.question: In a conductometric titration practical (e.g. strong acid vs strong base), the conductance of the solution initially decreases during the titration mainly because:
options: Highly mobile H+ ions are being progressively replaced by less mobile cations from the base
The volume of solution is decreasing
The temperature is decreasing sharply
No ions are present in solution
questions.correct_answer: Highly mobile H+ ions are being progressively replaced by less mobile cations from the base
questions.explanation: H+ ions have an unusually high ionic mobility; as they are neutralised and replaced by the less mobile cation of the base, overall conductance falls until the equivalence point.

questions.question: In a pH-metric titration practical, the equivalence point is most accurately located on the titration curve at the point where:
options: The pH is exactly 7 in every titration
The curve shows the steepest slope (point of inflection)
The volume of titrant added is zero
The pH stops changing entirely
questions.correct_answer: The curve shows the steepest slope (point of inflection)
questions.explanation: The equivalence point corresponds to the inflection point of the pH curve, where pH changes most rapidly per unit volume of titrant added; this need not be pH 7 unless a strong acid is titrated with a strong base.

questions.question: A calibration curve of absorbance versus concentration is constructed in a spectrophotometric practical before analysing an unknown mainly to:
options: Determine the unknown concentration by interpolating its measured absorbance on the standard curve
Clean the cuvette
Measure the melting point of the analyte
Replace the need for a blank measurement
questions.correct_answer: Determine the unknown concentration by interpolating its measured absorbance on the standard curve
questions.explanation: A set of standards of known concentration establishes the linear absorbance-concentration relationship, which is then used to read off the unknown's concentration from its measured absorbance.

questions.question: In an Ostwald viscometer practical, the relative viscosity of a test liquid compared to water is calculated using the ratio of:
options: (density x flow time) of the test liquid to (density x flow time) of water
Only the flow times, ignoring density
Only the densities, ignoring flow time
The boiling points of the two liquids
questions.correct_answer: (density x flow time) of the test liquid to (density x flow time) of water
questions.explanation: For an Ostwald viscometer under Poiseuille flow, relative viscosity is proportional to the product of density and flow time for each liquid, compared against the reference (water).

questions.question: Before titrating, a pipette is rinsed with the solution it will be used to measure, but a conical flask receiving the titrand is instead rinsed only with:
options: The titrant solution
Distilled water, since any residual water does not change the moles of titrand present
Concentrated acid
It should not be rinsed at all
questions.correct_answer: Distilled water, since any residual water does not change the moles of titrand present
questions.explanation: Water left in the flask does not add or remove moles of the substance being titrated, so rinsing with water (rather than the analyte solution) does not affect the titration's accuracy.

questions.question: A student records a titre value below the expected range for several repeat titrations. The most appropriate practical response is to:
options: Report the anomalous value without comment
Discard clearly outlying values, repeat the titration, and average only concordant results
Average all values including outliers regardless of spread
Increase the indicator volume to compensate
questions.correct_answer: Discard clearly outlying values, repeat the titration, and average only concordant results
questions.explanation: Good practical technique requires identifying and repeating anomalous titres, then averaging only concordant (closely agreeing) results to obtain a reliable titre value.

questions.question: Volumetric glassware such as pipettes and burettes are calibrated 'to deliver' (TD) or 'to contain' (TC); a graduated pipette marked TD is calibrated to:
options: Contain exactly the stated volume when filled, regardless of what is dispensed
Deliver the stated volume when allowed to drain under specified conditions
Measure gas volumes only
Measure mass rather than volume
questions.correct_answer: Deliver the stated volume when allowed to drain under specified conditions
questions.explanation: TD (to deliver) glassware is calibrated so that the stated volume is dispensed when the liquid is allowed to drain naturally, accounting for the film of liquid that clings to the walls.

questions.question: Systematic error in a titration practical, such as a consistently mis-calibrated burette, would primarily affect the:
options: Precision of the results without affecting accuracy
Accuracy of the results, shifting all measurements consistently in one direction even if precision (reproducibility) remains high
Colour of the indicator used
Only the first titration performed
questions.correct_answer: Accuracy of the results, shifting all measurements consistently in one direction even if precision (reproducibility) remains high
questions.explanation: Systematic errors bias every measurement in the same direction, reducing accuracy (closeness to the true value) while repeat measurements can still be precise (closely clustered around the biased value).

questions.question: Percentage error in an experimental result is calculated as:
options: (experimental value - true value) / true value x 100%, without regard to sign
experimental value x true value x 100%
true value / experimental value
experimental value - true value, expressed in the original units
questions.correct_answer: (experimental value - true value) / true value x 100%, without regard to sign
questions.explanation: Percentage error expresses the deviation of the measured value from the accepted true value as a percentage, usually reported as an absolute value.

questions.question: Before lighting a Bunsen burner near flammable organic solvents such as ether or acetone in the laboratory, the correct safety practice is to:
options: Proceed as normal since organic solvents are non-flammable
Ensure no open flames are present and use a water bath or electric heating mantle instead where possible
Increase the flame size for faster heating
Store the solvent bottle directly beside the flame
questions.correct_answer: Ensure no open flames are present and use a water bath or electric heating mantle instead where possible
questions.explanation: Many organic solvents are highly flammable and volatile; open flames must be avoided near them, with safer heating methods (water baths, heating mantles) used instead to prevent fire hazards.

questions.question: When diluting concentrated sulfuric acid with water in the laboratory, the correct and safe procedure is to:
options: Add water to the acid slowly
Add the acid slowly to water, with constant stirring
Mix both simultaneously from opposite sides of the vessel
Add the acid to water rapidly in one pour
questions.correct_answer: Add the acid slowly to water, with constant stirring
questions.explanation: Adding acid to water (rather than water to acid) allows the large heat of dilution to be absorbed by the larger volume of water, preventing dangerous spattering and boiling.

questions.question: In gravimetric analysis, a crucible must be ignited and cooled to constant weight before use mainly to:
options: Establish an accurate, reproducible blank (empty) mass of the crucible for later subtraction
Sterilise the crucible
Change the crucible's chemical composition
Add mass to the final precipitate
questions.correct_answer: Establish an accurate, reproducible blank (empty) mass of the crucible for later subtraction
questions.explanation: Pre-igniting and weighing the empty crucible to constant mass ensures a reliable baseline, so that the mass of precipitate obtained later (crucible + precipitate minus empty crucible) is accurate.

questions.question: A desiccator is used in gravimetric and other quantitative practical work mainly to:
options: Heat samples to high temperature
Cool and store dried/ignited samples in a moisture-free environment before weighing
Dissolve precipitates
Generate an inert gas atmosphere for reactions
questions.correct_answer: Cool and store dried/ignited samples in a moisture-free environment before weighing
questions.explanation: A desiccator contains a drying agent that maintains a low-humidity atmosphere, allowing hot samples to cool without reabsorbing atmospheric moisture, which would otherwise give a falsely high mass.

questions.question: In a standardisation practical, a primary standard substance such as anhydrous sodium carbonate is preferred because it is:
options: Highly hygroscopic and unstable in air
Available in high purity, stable, and of known, unchanging composition
Only usable for redox titrations
Impossible to weigh accurately
questions.correct_answer: Available in high purity, stable, and of known, unchanging composition
questions.explanation: Primary standards must be obtainable in very pure, stable form with a precisely known formula weight, allowing accurate preparation of standard solutions directly by weighing.
